layers.note: The tree of the snowiest subalpine forest and parkland, in clumps with subalpine fir.

moisture.note: Moist ground under a deep, late snowpack.

heat_load.note: Mostly cool, north-facing slopes where snow lies longest.

elevation_m.note: Sea level in Alaska; about 1,000 to 2,000 m in the Washington Cascades.

coldest_c.note: Across its range, coldest-month means from about −12 to 2 °C; gone below −20 °C and above 6 °C.

hard_freeze_c.note: Across its range, lows to about −35 °C borne, gone where the year's coldest night falls below about −42 °C.

warmest_c.note: Across its range, warmest-month means from about 8 to 16 °C; gone below 5 °C, where summers are too short, and above 19 °C.

degree_days_0.note: About 800 to 3,000 degree-days above 0 °C, none below 500.

degree_days_5.note: About 250 to 1,500 degree-days above 5 °C, none below 100.

moisture_index.note: A moisture index from about 0.7, gone by 0.5.

summer_rain.note: No lower limit: summer-dry Cascade summers suit it; up to about 0.5 of the year's precipitation in summer, gone by 0.7.

provenance.notes: Authored for the Mount Rainier subalpine meadow scene (Paradise, about 1,650 m) from general knowledge of the species; not yet checked against the public-domain USDA references (Silvics of North America, the Fire Effects Information System, PLANTS). Mountain hemlock grows from southern Alaska to the Sierra Nevada, in maritime mountain climates with deep snow (Silvics of North America). Each climate range brackets the climate of that range, an approximate envelope read from these descriptions, not fitted to occurrence records.
